**Invert Binary Tree** · Easy

You get the root of a binary tree. Turn the tree into its mirror image: at every node, the left subtree and the right subtree trade places. Return the root of the mirrored tree (the same root node).

**Constraints**
- 0 ≤ number of nodes ≤ 100
- −100 ≤ node value ≤ 100

**Example 1**

```tree
[4,2,7,1,3,6,9]
caption: input
```

Input: `root = [4,2,7,1,3,6,9]`
Output: `[4,7,2,9,6,3,1]`
Every level is read right to left after the flip: 2 and 7 swap, then 1/3 and 6/9 swap inside them.

**Example 2**
Input: `root = [2,1,3]` → Output: `[2,3,1]`

**Example 3**
Input: `root = []` → Output: `[]` (an empty tree stays empty)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/invert-a-binary-tree) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/invert-binary-tree/)

**Maximum Depth of Binary Tree** · Easy

You get the root of a binary tree. Its depth is the number of nodes on the longest path that starts at the root and goes down to a leaf. Return that number. An empty tree has depth 0.

**Constraints**
- 0 ≤ number of nodes ≤ 10⁴
- −100 ≤ node value ≤ 100

**Example 1**

```tree
[3*,9,20*,null,null,15*,7]
caption: longest path 3 → 20 → 15 has 3 nodes
```

Input: `root = [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`
Output: `3`
Both 3 → 20 → 15 and 3 → 20 → 7 have three nodes; the path to 9 has only two.

**Example 2**
Input: `root = [1,null,2]` → Output: `2` (the root plus its single right child)

**Example 3**
Input: `root = []` → Output: `0`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/depth-of-binary-tree) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-depth-of-binary-tree/)

**Diameter of Binary Tree** · Easy

You get the root of a binary tree. The diameter is the length of the longest path between any two nodes, counted in **edges**. The path may or may not pass through the root, and it can only use parent–child links. Return the diameter.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ number of nodes ≤ 10⁴
- −100 ≤ node value ≤ 100

**Example 1**

```tree
[1*,2*,3*,4*,5]
caption: 4 → 2 → 1 → 3 has 3 edges
```

Input: `root = [1,2,3,4,5]`
Output: `3`
The path 4 → 2 → 1 → 3 (or 5 → 2 → 1 → 3) uses three edges, and nothing is longer.

**Example 2**
Input: `root = [1,2]` → Output: `1`

**Example 3**

```tree
[1,2*,null,3*,4*,5*,null,null,6*]
caption: the longest path skips the root
```

Input: `root = [1,2,null,3,4,5,null,null,6]` → Output: `4` (5 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 6)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/binary-tree-diameter) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/diameter-of-binary-tree/)

**Balanced Binary Tree** · Easy

You get the root of a binary tree. Call it height-balanced if, at **every** node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. Return `true` if the tree is height-balanced, otherwise `false`. An empty tree counts as balanced.

**Constraints**
- 0 ≤ number of nodes ≤ 5000
- −10⁴ ≤ node value ≤ 10⁴

**Example 1**

```tree
[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]
```

Input: `root = [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`
Output: `true`
At the root the subtrees have heights 1 and 2; every other node is even closer.

**Example 2**

```tree
[1,2!,2,3,3,null,null,4,4]
caption: left height 3, right height 1 at the root
```

Input: `root = [1,2,2,3,3,null,null,4,4]`
Output: `false`

**Example 3**
Input: `root = []` → Output: `true`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/balanced-binary-tree) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/balanced-binary-tree/)

**Same Tree** · Easy

You get the roots `p` and `q` of two binary trees. They are the same if they have exactly the same shape and every pair of nodes in matching positions holds the same value. Return `true` if they are the same, otherwise `false`.

**Constraints**
- 0 ≤ nodes in each tree ≤ 100
- −10⁴ ≤ node value ≤ 10⁴

**Example 1**

```tree
[1,2,3]
caption: p and q are both this tree
```

Input: `p = [1,2,3], q = [1,2,3]`
Output: `true`

**Example 2**
Input: `p = [1,2], q = [1,null,2]` → Output: `false`
Same values, but 2 is a left child in `p` and a right child in `q`.

**Example 3**
Input: `p = [1,2,1], q = [1,1,2]` → Output: `false` (the children are swapped)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/same-binary-tree) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/same-tree/)

**Subtree of Another Tree** · Easy

You get the roots of two binary trees, `root` and `subRoot`. Return `true` if some node of `root` has a subtree that is identical to `subRoot` (same shape, same values, all the way down to the leaves). A node's subtree is that node plus all of its descendants; the whole tree counts as a subtree of itself.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ nodes in `root` ≤ 2000
- 1 ≤ nodes in `subRoot` ≤ 1000
- −10⁴ ≤ node value ≤ 10⁴

**Example 1**

```tree
[3,4*,5,1*,2*]
caption: root; subRoot = [4,1,2] matches the blue subtree
```

Input: `root = [3,4,5,1,2], subRoot = [4,1,2]`
Output: `true`

**Example 2**

```tree
[3,4!,5,1,2!,null,null,null,null,0!]
caption: the 4-subtree has an extra 0 below 2
```

Input: `root = [3,4,5,1,2,null,null,null,null,0], subRoot = [4,1,2]`
Output: `false`
A match must include every descendant, so the extra 0 breaks it.

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/subtree-of-a-binary-tree) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/subtree-of-another-tree/)

**Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree** · Medium

You get the root of a binary search tree (left subtree < node < right subtree, all values distinct) and two nodes `p` and `q` that are both in the tree. Return their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both `p` and `q` in its subtree. A node counts as an ancestor of itself, so if `p` is above `q`, the answer is `p`.

**Constraints**
- 2 ≤ number of nodes ≤ 10⁵
- −10⁹ ≤ node value ≤ 10⁹, all distinct
- `p != q`, both exist in the tree

**Example 1**

```tree
[6+,2*,8*,0,4,7,9,null,null,3,5]
caption: p = 2, q = 8 → they split at 6
```

Input: `root = [6,2,8,0,4,7,9,null,null,3,5], p = 2, q = 8`
Output: `6`

**Example 2**

```tree
[6,2+,8,0,4*,7,9,null,null,3,5]
caption: p = 2, q = 4 → 2 is an ancestor of 4
```

Input: same tree, `p = 2, q = 4`
Output: `2`

**Example 3**
Input: `root = [2,1], p = 2, q = 1` → Output: `2`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/lowest-common-ancestor-in-binary-search-tree) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-search-tree/)

**Binary Tree Level Order Traversal** · Medium

You get the root of a binary tree. Return its values grouped by level: one list for the root's level, one for the level below, and so on down. Inside each level, list the values from left to right. An empty tree gives an empty list.

**Constraints**
- 0 ≤ number of nodes ≤ 2000
- −1000 ≤ node value ≤ 1000

**Example 1**

```tree
[3*,9+,20+,null,null,15!,7!]
caption: one colour per level
```

Input: `root = [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`
Output: `[[3],[9,20],[15,7]]`

**Example 2**
Input: `root = [1]` → Output: `[[1]]`

**Example 3**
Input: `root = []` → Output: `[]`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/level-order-traversal-of-binary-tree) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/binary-tree-level-order-traversal/)

**Binary Tree Right Side View** · Medium

You get the root of a binary tree. Picture standing to the right of the tree and looking left: at each level you can see only the rightmost node. Return the values you can see, from the top level to the bottom one.

**Constraints**
- 0 ≤ number of nodes ≤ 100
- −100 ≤ node value ≤ 100

**Example 1**

```tree
[1*,2,3*,null,5,null,4*]
caption: visible from the right: 1, 3, 4
```

Input: `root = [1,2,3,null,5,null,4]`
Output: `[1,3,4]`

**Example 2**

```tree
[1*,2,3*,4*,null,null,null,5*]
caption: the left branch is deeper, so 4 and 5 show through
```

Input: `root = [1,2,3,4,null,null,null,5]`
Output: `[1,3,4,5]`

**Example 3**
Input: `root = []` → Output: `[]`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/binary-tree-right-side-view) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/binary-tree-right-side-view/)

**Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree** · Medium

You get the root of a binary tree. A node is **good** if, on the path from the root down to that node, no node has a value larger than it. The root is always good. Return the number of good nodes.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ number of nodes ≤ 10⁵
- −10⁴ ≤ node value ≤ 10⁴

**Example 1**

```tree
[3+,1,4+,3+,null,1,5+]
caption: good nodes in green
```

Input: `root = [3,1,4,3,null,1,5]`
Output: `4`
The root 3, the 4, the 5 below it, and the lower-left 3 (its path 3 → 1 → 3 has nothing above 3) are good. The 1s are not.

**Example 2**
Input: `root = [3,3,null,4,2]` → Output: `3` (equal values count as good; only 2 is not)

**Example 3**
Input: `root = [1]` → Output: `1`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/count-good-nodes-in-binary-tree) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/count-good-nodes-in-binary-tree/)

**Validate Binary Search Tree** · Medium

You get the root of a binary tree. Decide whether it is a valid binary search tree: for every node, **all** values in its left subtree are strictly smaller than it, **all** values in its right subtree are strictly larger, and both subtrees are valid BSTs themselves. Return `true` or `false`.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ number of nodes ≤ 10⁴
- −2³¹ ≤ node value ≤ 2³¹ − 1

**Example 1**

```tree
[2,1,3]
```

Input: `root = [2,1,3]` → Output: `true`

**Example 2**

```tree
[5,1,4!,null,null,3!,6]
caption: 4 sits in 5's right subtree but is smaller than 5
```

Input: `root = [5,1,4,null,null,3,6]`
Output: `false`

**Example 3**

```tree
[5,4,6,null,null,3!,7]
caption: every parent-child pair is fine, but 3 < 5 is in 5's right subtree
```

Input: `root = [5,4,6,null,null,3,7]` → Output: `false`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/valid-binary-search-tree) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/validate-binary-search-tree/)

**Kth Smallest Element in a BST** · Medium

You get the root of a binary search tree and an integer `k` (1-indexed). Return the `k`-th smallest value stored in the tree: `k = 1` is the minimum, `k = n` the maximum.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 10⁴
- 0 ≤ node value ≤ 10⁴

**Example 1**

```tree
[3,1*,4,null,2]
caption: sorted: 1 2 3 4
```

Input: `root = [3,1,4,null,2], k = 1`
Output: `1`

**Example 2**

```tree
[5,3*,6,2,4,null,null,1]
caption: sorted: 1 2 3 4 5 6 → 3rd is 3
```

Input: `root = [5,3,6,2,4,null,null,1], k = 3`
Output: `3`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/kth-smallest-integer-in-bst) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst/)

**Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal** · Medium

You get two integer arrays describing the same binary tree: `preorder` (node, then left subtree, then right subtree) and `inorder` (left subtree, then node, then right subtree). All values are distinct. Rebuild the tree and return its root.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ n ≤ 3000, both arrays have length n
- −3000 ≤ value ≤ 3000, all values distinct
- the arrays are guaranteed to come from one valid tree

**Example 1**

```tree
[3*,9,20,null,null,15,7]
caption: preorder starts with the root, 3
```

Input: `preorder = [3,9,20,15,7], inorder = [9,3,15,20,7]`
Output: `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`
3 comes first in preorder, so it is the root. In inorder, `[9]` sits left of 3 (left subtree) and `[15,20,7]` sits right of it (right subtree).

**Example 2**
Input: `preorder = [-1], inorder = [-1]` → Output: `[-1]`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/binary-tree-from-preorder-and-inorder-traversal) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-inorder-traversal/)

**Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum** · Hard

You get the root of a binary tree whose values can be negative. A path is any sequence of nodes where neighbours in the sequence are parent and child, and no node appears twice. It must contain at least one node and does not have to pass through the root. Return the largest possible sum of the values on a path.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ number of nodes ≤ 3·10⁴
- −1000 ≤ node value ≤ 1000

**Example 1**

```tree
[1*,2*,3*]
caption: 2 → 1 → 3
```

Input: `root = [1,2,3]` → Output: `6`

**Example 2**

```tree
[-10,9,20*,null,null,15*,7*]
caption: best path 15 → 20 → 7 skips the root
```

Input: `root = [-10,9,20,null,null,15,7]`
Output: `42`
Going through −10 would only lower the sum.

**Example 3**
Input: `root = [-3]` → Output: `-3` (the path must have at least one node)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/binary-tree-maximum-path-sum) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/binary-tree-maximum-path-sum/)

**Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree** · Hard

Design a `Codec` class with two methods. `serialize(root)` turns a binary tree into a string; `deserialize(data)` turns that string back into a tree. The format is up to you. The only requirement: deserializing what you serialized must give back a tree with exactly the same shape and values.

**Constraints**
- 0 ≤ number of nodes ≤ 10⁴
- −1000 ≤ node value ≤ 1000

**Example 1**

```tree
[1,2,3,null,null,4,5]
```

Input: `root = [1,2,3,null,null,4,5]`
Output: `[1,2,3,null,null,4,5]`
For example, pre-order with `N` for empty children gives `"1,2,N,N,3,4,N,N,5,N,N"`, and reading it back rebuilds the same tree.

**Example 2**
Input: `root = []` → Output: `[]`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/serialize-and-deserialize-binary-tree) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/serialize-and-deserialize-binary-tree/)

**Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)** · Medium

Build a `Trie` class that stores lowercase words and answers prefix questions:
- `Trie()` creates an empty trie.
- `insert(word)` adds `word`.
- `search(word)` returns `true` only if exactly `word` was inserted before.
- `startsWith(prefix)` returns `true` if any inserted word begins with `prefix`.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ word / prefix length ≤ 2000, lowercase English letters
- at most 3·10⁴ calls in total

**Example 1**

```list
root -> a -> p -> p+ -> l -> e+
caption: after inserting "apple" and "app": one path of child links (green = end of a word)
```

Input: `["Trie","insert","search","search","startsWith","insert","search"]`, `[[],["apple"],["apple"],["app"],["app"],["app"],["app"]]`
Output: `[null,null,true,false,true,null,true]`
"app" is only a prefix until it is inserted itself; after that `search("app")` is true.

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/implement-prefix-tree) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/implement-trie-prefix-tree/)

**Design Add and Search Words Data Structure** · Medium

Build a `WordDictionary` class:
- `WordDictionary()` starts empty.
- `addWord(word)` stores a lowercase word.
- `search(word)` returns `true` if some stored word matches `word`. The query may contain `.`, which matches any single letter; other letters must match exactly, and the lengths must be equal.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ word length ≤ 25
- added words are lowercase letters; queries are lowercase letters or `.`
- at most 2 dots per query, at most 10⁴ calls

**Example 1**
Input: `["WordDictionary","addWord","addWord","addWord","search","search","search","search"]`, `[[],["bad"],["dad"],["mad"],["pad"],["bad"],[".ad"],["b.."]]`
Output: `[null,null,null,null,false,true,true,true]`
"pad" was never added; ".ad" matches bad/dad/mad; "b.." matches bad.

**Example 2**
After `addWord("a")`: `search(".")` → `true`, `search("..")` → `false` (lengths differ)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/design-word-search-data-structure) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/design-add-and-search-words-data-structure/)

**Word Search II** · Hard

You get an m × n board of lowercase letters and a list of distinct words. A word can be formed by starting on any cell and repeatedly stepping to a cell above, below, left or right, reading one letter per cell; a single word may not use the same cell twice. Return every word from the list that can be formed on the board, in any order.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ m, n ≤ 12
- 1 ≤ number of words ≤ 3·10⁴, each 1–10 lowercase letters, all distinct

**Example 1**

```grid
o* a* a n
e t* a! e!
i h* k r
i f l v
caption: blue spells oath; orange spells eat, sharing the blue t
```

Input: `board = [["o","a","a","n"],["e","t","a","e"],["i","h","k","r"],["i","f","l","v"]], words = ["oath","pea","eat","rain"]`
Output: `["eat","oath"]`
"pea" and "rain" can't be traced along adjacent cells.

**Example 2**
Input: `board = [["a","b"],["c","d"]], words = ["abcb"]` → Output: `[]`
Spelling it would need to reuse the "b" cell.

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/search-for-word-ii) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/word-search-ii/)

**Kth Largest Element in a Stream** · Easy

Build a `KthLargest` class for a stream of scores:
- `KthLargest(k, nums)` starts with the integer `k` and an initial list of numbers.
- `add(val)` appends `val` to the stream and returns the `k`-th largest number seen so far (counting duplicates, so it's the k-th in sorted order, not the k-th distinct value).

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ k ≤ 10⁴, 0 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁴
- −10⁴ ≤ values ≤ 10⁴, at most 10⁴ calls to `add`
- there are always at least `k` numbers when `add` returns

**Example 1**
Input: `["KthLargest","add","add","add","add","add"]`, `[[3,[4,5,8,2]],[3],[5],[10],[9],[4]]`
Output: `[null,4,5,5,8,8]`
After adding 3 the stream is 2 3 4 5 8, and the 3rd largest is 4. Adding 5 gives 2 3 4 5 5 8 → 5, and so on.

**Example 2**
Input: `["KthLargest","add","add","add","add"]`, `[[4,[7,7,7,7,8,3]],[2],[10],[9],[9]]`
Output: `[null,7,7,7,8]`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/kth-largest-integer-in-a-stream) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/kth-largest-element-in-a-stream/)

**Last Stone Weight** · Easy

You get an array of positive stone weights. Repeatedly take the two heaviest stones, `y ≥ x`, and smash them: if they weigh the same, both disappear; otherwise only a stone of weight `y − x` remains. Stop when at most one stone is left. Return its weight, or `0` if none are left.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ stones.length ≤ 30
- 1 ≤ stones[i] ≤ 1000

**Example 1**
Input: `stones = [2,7,4,1,8,1]`
Output: `1`
8 vs 7 → 1, leaving [2,4,1,1,1]; 4 vs 2 → 2, leaving [2,1,1,1]; 2 vs 1 → 1, leaving [1,1,1]; 1 vs 1 → nothing, leaving [1].

**Example 2**
Input: `stones = [1]` → Output: `1`

**Example 3**
Input: `stones = [3,3]` → Output: `0`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/last-stone-weight) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/last-stone-weight/)

**K Closest Points to Origin** · Medium

You get a list of points `[x, y]` on a plane and an integer `k`. Return the `k` points nearest to the origin (0, 0) by ordinary straight-line distance. The output can be in any order; the inputs guarantee the answer is unique (no tie at the cut-off).

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ k ≤ points.length ≤ 10⁴
- −10⁴ ≤ x, y ≤ 10⁴

**Example 1**
Input: `points = [[1,3],[-2,2]], k = 1`
Output: `[[-2,2]]`
Squared distances are 1 + 9 = 10 and 4 + 4 = 8, so (−2, 2) is closer.

**Example 2**
Input: `points = [[3,3],[5,-1],[-2,4]], k = 2`
Output: `[[3,3],[-2,4]]` (squared distances 18, 26, 20; any order is accepted)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/k-closest-points-to-origin) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/k-closest-points-to-origin/)

**Kth Largest Element in an Array** · Medium

You get an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. Return the `k`-th largest element: the value that would be at position `k` if the array were sorted from largest to smallest. Duplicates count separately (it is not the k-th *distinct* value). Try to do better than sorting.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ k ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵
- −10⁴ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴

**Example 1**
Input: `nums = [3,2,1,5,6,4], k = 2`
Output: `5`
Largest first: 6, 5, 4, … so the 2nd is 5.

**Example 2**
Input: `nums = [3,2,3,1,2,4,5,5,6], k = 4`
Output: `4`
Largest first: 6, 5, 5, 4, … The two 5s count as two places.

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/kth-largest-element-in-an-array) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/kth-largest-element-in-an-array/)

**Task Scheduler** · Medium

You get a list of CPU tasks, each an uppercase letter, and a cooldown `n`. Each time unit the CPU either runs one task or sits idle. Two runs of the **same** letter must be at least `n` time units apart (at least `n` other slots between them). Tasks may run in any order. Return the minimum number of time units needed to finish all of them.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ tasks.length ≤ 10⁴
- tasks[i] is `A`–`Z`
- 0 ≤ n ≤ 100

**Example 1**
Input: `tasks = ["A","A","A","B","B","B"], n = 2`
Output: `8`
One best order: A B idle A B idle A B. Each A is 3 slots after the previous A.

**Example 2**
Input: `tasks = ["A","C","A","B","D","B"], n = 1`
Output: `6`
A B C A D B needs no idle slots.

**Example 3**
Input: `tasks = ["A","A","A","B","B","B"], n = 3` → Output: `10` (A B idle idle A B idle idle A B)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/task-scheduling) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/task-scheduler/)

**Design Twitter** · Medium

Build a tiny `Twitter`:
- `postTweet(userId, tweetId)` posts a new tweet with a unique id. Every call is newer than all earlier calls.
- `getNewsFeed(userId)` returns up to 10 of the most recent tweet ids posted by the user or by anyone they follow, newest first.
- `follow(followerId, followeeId)` / `unfollow(followerId, followeeId)` start or stop following. Unfollowing someone you don't follow does nothing.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ userId, followerId, followeeId ≤ 500
- 0 ≤ tweetId ≤ 10⁴, all tweet ids unique
- at most 3·10⁴ calls in total

**Example 1**
Input: `["Twitter","postTweet","getNewsFeed","follow","postTweet","getNewsFeed","unfollow","getNewsFeed"]`, `[[],[1,5],[1],[1,2],[2,6],[1],[1,2],[1]]`
Output: `[null,null,[5],null,null,[6,5],null,[5]]`
User 1 posts 5 and sees `[5]`. After following user 2, who posts 6, the feed is `[6,5]`. After unfollowing, only `[5]` remains.

**Example 2**
